templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Mistletoes are parasitic plants that grow in the branches of trees and offer fruit and nectar that many birds consume. Ecologists have long described them as a keystone resource in the eucalyptus woodlands of Australia. To test that description, David Watson and Matthew Herring removed every mistletoe plant from 17 woodlands and compared those sites with woodlands where the plants were left alone. Three years later, the woodlands cleared of mistletoe had lost about a fifth of their bird species, but the species recorded feeding on mistletoe had fared no worse there than in the untouched woodlands.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about mistletoe in the woodlands that Watson and Herring studied?
options: It likely contributes little to the variety of birds in these woodlands, since the birds that feed on it fared no worse after its removal than birds in untouched woodlands did.
It likely supports the variety of birds in these woodlands mainly by feeding them, since the woodlands lost about a fifth of their bird species after it was removed.
It likely sustains many of the woodlands’ bird species in some way other than through the fruit and nectar it offers to the birds that eat them.
It likely attracts fruit-eating birds whose presence in turn draws the other bird species that disappeared from the woodlands after it was removed.
items.explanation: Removing the mistletoe clearly mattered: the cleared woodlands “had lost about a fifth of their bird species.” Yet “the species recorded feeding on mistletoe had fared no worse there than in the untouched woodlands,” so the losses were not concentrated among the birds that eat it. Together these facts suggest that mistletoe supports many bird species through something other than the fruit and nectar it provides.

A.why_wrong: The mistletoe feeders did fare no worse, but the woodlands still lost about a fifth of their bird species once the mistletoe was gone, so the plant contributes a great deal.

B.why_wrong: The woodlands did lose about a fifth of their species, but the birds that feed on mistletoe fared no worse than elsewhere, so the loss cannot be explained mainly by the food mistletoe provides.

D.why_wrong: If fruit eaters drew the other species, the other species should have stayed as long as the fruit eaters did; instead the fruit eaters fared no worse while other species disappeared, and the text never describes one group attracting another.

sources.what: Watson and Herring 2012, Proc R Soc B: all mistletoe removed from 17 eucalypt woodland sites; after three years treatment sites lost 20.9% of total species richness; changes in species recorded feeding on mistletoe did not differ from control sites (PMC3415901)

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). P1: removal cost about a fifth of bird species; P2: mistletoe feeders fared no worse than in control woodlands; unstated conclusion: mistletoe's value works through something besides its fruit and nectar (the authors suggest leaf litter, which the passage leaves out). Nesting losses also left out so no option can lean on them. Band 6 target: every distractor keeps a true detail and fails on the link drawn from it.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from an 1887 translation of Alphonse Daudet’s 1872 novel Tartarin of Tarascon. The narrator describes the garden of Tartarin, a man who lives in the small French town of Tarascon.

Not a native tree was there—not one flower of France; nothing but exotic plants, gum-trees, gourds, cotton-woods, cocoa and cacao, mangoes, bananas, palms, a baobab, nopals, cacti, Barbary figs—well, you would believe yourself in the very midst of Central Africa, ten thousand leagues away. It is but fair to say that these were none of full growth; indeed, the cocoa-palms were no bigger than beet root and the baobab (arbos gigantea—“giant tree,” you know) was easily enough circumscribed by a window-pot; but, notwithstanding this, it was rather a sensation for Tarascon, and the townsfolk who were admitted on Sundays to the honour of contemplating Tartarin’s baobab, went home chokeful of admiration.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is most likely true about the townsfolk of Tarascon who visit the garden?
options: They are more easily impressed than the garden’s modest plants would seem to justify.
They value the garden chiefly because Tartarin allows them to see it only on Sundays.
They privately find the garden absurd, though they praise it to Tartarin out of politeness.
They have seen enough of Central Africa to recognize how faithfully the garden imitates it.
items.explanation: The narrator admits that the garden’s plants “were none of full growth”: the palms “were no bigger than beet root,” and the “giant tree” fits in “a window-pot.” Even so, the garden was “a sensation for Tarascon,” and visitors “went home chokeful of admiration.” The gap between the tiny plants and the townsfolk’s delight suggests that they are easily impressed.

B.why_wrong: Visitors are indeed “admitted on Sundays,” but the text never suggests that limited access is why they admire the garden; it ties their admiration to the exotic plants themselves.

C.why_wrong: The narrator gently mocks the garden, but the townsfolk “went home chokeful of admiration,” which shows sincere delight, not hidden scorn.

D.recipe: twisted detail (narrator's remark given to the townsfolk)
D.why_wrong: It is the narrator who says “you would believe yourself in the very midst of Central Africa,” and he says it ironically; nothing indicates that the townsfolk have been to Africa, and the stunted plants are not faithful copies.

sources.what: Daudet, Tartarin of Tarascon (Project Gutenberg #1862, English translation), chapter I, The Garden Round the Giant Trees
Same translation in the 1887 Routledge edition, Tartarin of Tarascon: Traveller, “Turk,” and Lion-Hunter; the title page names no translator

items.notes: Literary irony (T6 literary variant). Excerpt copied from Gutenberg #1862; adaptations: Gutenberg typo 'hut' corrected to 'but', double hyphens set as closed em dashes, first two exclamatory sentences trimmed. Gutenberg names no translator, so the source line gives none. P1: plants stunted, giant tree in a pot; P2: townsfolk full of admiration; conclusion: they are easily impressed. Reviewer: the translation is anonymous (1887 Routledge and 1896 Dent editions carry the same text and name no translator), so the source line rightly names none.

fixes: excerpt checked against Gutenberg #1862: exact apart from the noted typo fix, dashes and trim; translation confirmed anonymous (1887 Routledge scan, no translator on the title page), so no translator in the source line
source line now reads “adapted from an 1887 translation of”, CB’s form for a translation (as in its Molloy line), since the translator is anonymous

items.passage: The earliest whales, which walked on four legs, originated in South Asia more than 50 million years ago, and fossil evidence indicates that these amphibious mammals subsequently dispersed westward along the coast of North Africa. In 2019 Olivier Lambert and colleagues described Peregocetus pacificus, a whale whose 42.6-million-year-old skeleton was discovered in coastal Peru, across the South Atlantic Ocean from Africa. Its pelvis was firmly attached to its spine, and its toes terminated in small hooves; it therefore could still stand and walk on land. Its broad tail vertebrae, however, resemble those of otters and beavers, which use their tails for swimming.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about early whales?
options: Some of them likely could not have reached South America until their bodies had become fully suited to life in the water.
Some of them likely reached South America by walking along coastlines, because they could still stand and walk on land.
Those in South America likely swam better than those in South Asia did, since Peregocetus had tail vertebrae like those of otters.
Some of them likely crossed a broad stretch of ocean while they still had legs that could support them on land.
items.explanation: The text says that four-legged whales spread along “the coast of North Africa” and that Peregocetus was found in Peru, “across the South Atlantic Ocean from Africa.” It also says Peregocetus “could still stand and walk on land.” Together these details suggest that some early whales crossed an ocean while they could still move about on land.

A.why_wrong: Early whales did eventually become fully aquatic, but Peregocetus reached Peru while it “could still stand and walk on land,” so a fully aquatic body was not required.

B.why_wrong: Peregocetus could walk, but Peru lies “across the South Atlantic Ocean from Africa,” so whales could not have walked there along a coastline from North Africa.

C.why_wrong: The otter-like tail vertebrae suggest that Peregocetus swam with its tail, but the text never compares its swimming with that of the South Asian whales.

sources.what: Lambert et al. 2019, Current Biology: cetaceans originated in south Asia more than 50 mya; amphibious whales dispersed westward along North Africa; Peregocetus pacificus, 42.6 mya, coastal Peru, pelvis firmly attached to sacrum, small hooves, otter-like caudal vertebrae; demonstrates that early quadrupedal whales crossed the South Atlantic (PMID 30955933)

items.notes: Natural science (paleontology). P1: four-legged whales spread from South Asia along North Africa; P2: Peregocetus, still able to walk, reached Peru across the South Atlantic; unstated conclusion: quadrupedal whales crossed open ocean (the paper's own conclusion, not stated in the passage). Feet: paper says fingers and toes; passage says toes.

fixes: band 6 kept as written: A (could still walk) and B (ocean in between) each fall to one stated fact, but the key needs the origin, the route and the walking ability together, and the coastal-walk trap is intuitive; no rebuild that keeps one answer

items.passage: In 1801 the Joseon court of Korea published the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, a ten-volume record documenting the construction of Hwaseong Fortress in the city of Suwon. In addition to royal orders, the record contains architectural plans of the fortress, inventories of the quantities of materials consumed, and the wages paid to its foremen, stonemasons, and laborers. During the Korean War the fortress was severely damaged, and most of what visitors encounter today is a reconstruction carried out in the 1970s. Nevertheless, UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1997, a distinction rarely granted to a structure that is largely a modern reconstruction.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the rebuilding of Hwaseong Fortress in the 1970s?
options: It likely drew more on the record’s inventories of materials and wages than on its plans, since the record lists the wages paid to each kind of worker.
It likely followed the 1801 record so closely that the rebuilt fortress could be regarded as true to the original one.
It likely produced a fortress sturdier than the original, since UNESCO honored the fortress even though most of it is a reconstruction.
It likely relied on the 1801 record because the war had destroyed every other image of the fortress that had been made before it.
items.explanation: The text says that the 1801 record includes “architectural plans of the fortress” and “inventories of the quantities of materials consumed,” and that although most of the fortress is “a reconstruction carried out in the 1970s,” UNESCO still honored it, a distinction “rarely granted to a structure that is largely a modern reconstruction.” These details suggest that the rebuilding followed the detailed record closely enough for the fortress to count as faithful to the original.

A.why_wrong: The record does list materials and wages, but the text never compares how much the builders used those lists with how much they used the plans.

C.why_wrong: UNESCO did honor the largely rebuilt fortress, but the text says nothing about its strength; the honor points to faithfulness to the original, not sturdiness.

D.why_wrong: The builders may well have used the record, but the text never says that all other images of the fortress were lost in the war.

sources.what: Hwaseong Fortress (Wikipedia): Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe published 1801, ten volumes, plans, wages, quantities of materials; invaluable for the 1970s reconstruction after Korean War damage; listed by UNESCO in 1997 despite being a modern restored building

items.notes: History (architecture). P1: the 1801 record holds plans and material quantities; P2: the fortress is mostly a 1970s rebuild yet won an honor rarely given to reconstructions; unstated conclusion: the rebuild followed the record faithfully (the source says the record proved invaluable for it). The source's 'king' is King Jeongjo, left unnamed to save words.

items.passage: Small talk between strangers can seem too trivial to study, but Karen Huang and colleagues recorded and analyzed such conversations, from online chats to face-to-face speed dates, to determine what makes a conversation partner likable. People who asked more questions, particularly follow-up questions that build on what a partner has just said, were better liked, apparently because such questions demonstrate attentiveness and concern. Speed daters who asked more follow-up questions were also more frequently granted second dates. Yet the researchers also found that people do not expect asking questions to make others like them more.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research suggests that asking questions, especially ones that pick up on what a partner has said, makes people more likable, though people tend not to realize that it does.
Research suggests that follow-up questions make people more likable than other kinds of questions do, a difference that most people already expect when they talk with strangers.
Huang and colleagues found that asking questions made people more likable in online chats between strangers but had little effect in face-to-face conversations such as speed dates.
Huang and colleagues found that asking questions made people better liked mainly because it gave their partners more time to talk about themselves.
items.explanation: The text reports that people “who asked more questions, particularly follow-up questions,” were “better liked,” and it then adds that “people do not expect asking questions to make others like them more.” Choice A states both parts of this finding.

B.why_wrong: Follow-up questions did matter most, but the text says people “do not expect” questions to raise liking, so the claim that people already expect the difference contradicts it.

C.why_wrong: The effect did appear online, but it also appeared in speed dates, where daters who asked more follow-up questions were “more frequently granted second dates.”

D.why_wrong: People who asked more questions were indeed “better liked,” but the text explains this “apparently because such questions demonstrate attentiveness and concern,” not because partners had more time to talk; the choice also leaves out the finding that people “do not expect” questions to raise liking.

sources.what: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson, Gino 2017, JPSP, It doesn't hurt to ask: question-asking, particularly follow-up questions, increases liking; responsiveness explains it; speed daters who ask more follow-up questions more often get second dates; people do not anticipate that question-asking increases liking (original abstract reprinted in the 2025 correction notice, which reports an audit confirming all conclusions)

items.notes: Social science (psychology). Frame check: the misprediction half resembles the social-misprediction frame of Kumar and Epley (CoE w2b2_02), for which a compliments item was once withdrawn; kept because the study and finding (question-asking, follow-up questions, responsiveness) are distinct and the two-part key needs the twist. Two-part key (finding plus the misprediction), as in 3.9 and 3.21. Key paraphrases 'follow-up questions that build on' as 'pick up on what a partner has said'. The paper had a 2025 correction after an independent audit that confirmed every conclusion; Gino is left unnamed.

fixes: hardened to band 6: D (reversed cause, no true part) now keeps the true liking finding and fails on the mechanism (talk time instead of attentiveness); re-solved blind, A only

frame judged against Kumar and Epley (CoE w2b2_02) and Kardas, Kumar and Epley (CoE w3b7_10): kept, since the behaviour (question-asking), lab and design differ and the misprediction is only the second half of the key; core claim checked on the 2025 correction notice (audit confirmed all conclusions)

items.passage: Muslim printers in the Ottoman Empire did not produce books in Arabic script on a substantial scale until the nineteenth century, and for generations historians attributed this delay to a prohibition on printing supposedly issued by two Ottoman sultans. Historian Kathryn Schwartz, however, has traced accounts of the prohibition to a rumor originating in early modern Europe. According to Schwartz, nineteenth-century Ottoman writers adopted the European account, and twentieth-century historians subsequently repeated it until it came to be treated as established fact.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although Schwartz doubts that the sultans ever banned printing, she argues that the late rise of Arabic-script printing is better explained by the small demand for books among Ottoman readers.
Although the ban was first described by European writers, Schwartz shows that nineteenth-century Ottoman writers later found evidence that the ban had been issued.
Although the ban on printing began as a European rumor, Schwartz argues that it was enforced mainly against European printers working in the Ottoman Empire.
Although historians long blamed a ban by two sultans for the late rise of Ottoman Arabic-script printing, Schwartz argues that the ban began as a European rumor later accepted as fact.
items.explanation: The text says that historians long “attributed this delay to a prohibition on printing supposedly issued by two Ottoman sultans,” but that Schwartz “has traced accounts of the prohibition to a rumor originating in early modern Europe,” which later writers repeated “until it came to be treated as established fact.” Choice D captures both the long-held explanation and Schwartz’s revision of it.

A.why_wrong: Schwartz does trace the ban to “a rumor originating in early modern Europe,” but the text never says she offers another cause for the delay, such as demand for books; it is about how the rumor came to be “treated as established fact.”

B.why_wrong: The account did begin in Europe, but nineteenth-century Ottoman writers merely “adopted the European account”; the text mentions no evidence they found.

C.why_wrong: The story did begin as a European rumor, but the text gives no sign that any ban was enforced, against European printers or anyone else.

sources.what: Schwartz, Did Ottoman Sultans Ban Print?, Book History 2017 (doi 10.1353/bh.2017.0000): charts the life cycle of the rumor that two Ottoman sultans banned print, from early modern Europe, adopted by nineteenth-century Ottomans, stabilized through twentieth-century historians (abstract via OpenAlex)
Same article, publisher page on Project MUSE (abstract; blocks scripted access)
Global spread of the printing press (Wikipedia): Muslim Arabic-script printing in the Ottoman Empire did not really take off until the nineteenth century

items.notes: History. View then correction. The abstract is on the OpenAlex record (Project MUSE blocks scripted access). Passage keeps the source's word 'rumor' and does not claim more than that.

fixes: hardened to band 6: A was killed by its first clause (the sultans did ban printing); now a true first part (Schwartz doubts the ban) failing on an invented demand explanation
key reworded: the ungrammatical “a sultans’ ban” replaced and the key paraphrased away from “traced ... rumor ... established fact”; re-solved blind, D only
key trimmed so it is no longer the longest option

items.passage: Ziryab, a musician who joined the court of Córdoba in 822, is frequently credited with transforming daily life in al-Andalus. According to tradition, he introduced clothing appropriate to each season, fashionable new hairstyles, an early toothpaste, and meals served in separate courses. Yet some claims about him, such as that he opened beauty parlors for women of the court, are not supported by the earliest sources. Moreover, historian Henri Terrasse contended that the transformation in dress credited to Ziryab was too sweeping for a single individual to have accomplished, reflecting instead a development occurring throughout the Muslim world.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although Ziryab came to Córdoba as a musician, he is now remembered mainly for his influence on clothing and manners rather than for his music.
Although later accounts exaggerate Ziryab’s influence on dress, historians agree that he did introduce the early toothpaste and the meal served in courses.
Although Ziryab is widely credited with reshaping customs in al-Andalus, some of those changes likely owed more to broader developments than to him alone.
Although Terrasse doubted that Ziryab changed styles of dress himself, he argued that the new styles spread from al-Andalus to the rest of the Muslim world.
items.explanation: The text first says that Ziryab “is frequently credited with transforming daily life in al-Andalus.” It then qualifies that reputation: some claims about him “are not supported by the earliest sources,” and Terrasse contended that the change in dress reflected “a development occurring throughout the Muslim world.” Choice C states both the reputation and the doubt about it.

A.why_wrong: The text lists the customs credited to Ziryab, but it never says he is remembered more for them than for his music.

B.why_wrong: The text does question his influence on dress, but it never says historians agree about the toothpaste or the meals; it notes only that some claims about him are not supported by the earliest sources.

D.why_wrong: Terrasse saw the change in dress as part of “a development occurring throughout the Muslim world,” not as something that spread outward from al-Andalus.

sources.what: Ziryab (Wikipedia): arrived in Córdoba 822; credited with seasonal clothing, hairstyles, toothpaste, three-course meals; some claims (beauty parlors) not supported by the early sources; Henri Terrasse: a lone man could not achieve this transformation in dress, rather a development across the Muslim world

items.notes: Arts and humanities (music history). Terrasse's view is paraphrased, not quoted. The beauty-parlor example is the source's own case of a claim not supported by the early sources; the passage names only that case.

items.passage: Born into a wealthy family in 1789, Leona Vicario became one of the most prominent supporters of Mexico’s war for independence from Spain. As a member of Los Guadalupes, a secret society, she relayed insurgent correspondence, kept the rebels informed about developments in Mexico City, the colonial capital, and sent them money and medicine. When her activities were discovered in 1813, she was detained and interrogated but refused to identify the other conspirators. After insurgents helped her escape, the colonial authorities confiscated her property.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about Vicario’s role in the independence movement?
options: She commanded insurgent troops in several battles fought near the colonial capital.
She assisted the rebels by passing along their messages and providing them with supplies.
She founded Los Guadalupes and paid for the society’s activities with her family’s fortune.
She gave the authorities the names of other conspirators in exchange for her release.
items.explanation: The text says that Vicario “relayed insurgent correspondence” and “sent them money and medicine.” In other words, she helped the rebels by passing along messages and supplying them.

A.why_wrong: The text describes Vicario carrying messages and sending supplies; it never says she led troops in battle.

C.why_wrong: Vicario was “a member of Los Guadalupes,” not its founder, and the text never says her family’s fortune paid for the society.

D.why_wrong: The text says she “refused to identify the other conspirators,” and she gained her freedom when insurgents helped her escape.

sources.what: Leona Vicario (Wikipedia): member of Los Guadalupes; received and distributed insurgent correspondence, informed insurgents of events in Mexico City, sent money and medicine; detained and questioned in 1813, refused to inform on the conspirators; rescued by insurgents; property confiscated

items.notes: History (Mexico). Explicit detail; key joins two clauses of one sentence and abstracts them (messages, supplies).

items.passage: On October 6, 2008, astronomer Richard Kowalski detected a small asteroid, later designated 2008 TC3, about twenty hours before it entered Earth’s atmosphere; it was the first time an asteroid’s impact had been predicted in advance. Observers tracked its path and measured the sunlight reflected from its surface before it exploded above the Nubian Desert in Sudan. Two months later, Peter Jenniskens and Muawia Shaddad led a search with students from the University of Khartoum that recovered fragments of the asteroid. For the first time, scientists could connect a particular class of asteroid with a specific type of meteorite.
items.stem: According to the text, what made it possible for scientists to connect a class of asteroid with a type of meteorite?
options: Researchers studied the asteroid in space and later recovered pieces of it on the ground.
The asteroid broke apart high above the desert, so its fragments landed close together.
Students in Sudan had already collected similar meteorites in the Nubian Desert before 2008.
Kowalski calculated the exact spot in Sudan where the asteroid’s fragments would come to rest.
items.explanation: The text says that observers “measured the sunlight reflected from its surface” while the asteroid was still in space and that a later search “recovered fragments of the asteroid.” Having both kinds of information let scientists, “For the first time,” match a class of asteroid with a type of meteorite.

B.why_wrong: The text says the asteroid exploded above the desert but says nothing about how closely its fragments landed or links that to the scientists’ match.

C.why_wrong: The students took part in the search two months after the impact; the text never mentions earlier collections of similar meteorites.

D.why_wrong: Kowalski detected the asteroid; the text does not say he predicted exactly where its fragments would land.

sources.what: 2008 TC3 (Wikipedia): discovered by Richard Kowalski about 20 hours before impact, the first asteroid impact predicted before entry; spectral and photometric observations; exploded over the Nubian Desert; search led by Peter Jenniskens and Muawia Shaddad with University of Khartoum students recovered the Almahata Sitta meteorites; for the first time asteroid class and meteorite type were linked

items.notes: Natural science (astronomy). The two facts the key joins sit in sentences 2 and 3; the last sentence states the result the stem names.

fixes: premise confirmed on the source: astronomical observations plus the recovered meteorites linked asteroid class and meteorite type for the first time

items.passage: Dancer Michio Itō left Japan as a teenager to study music in Paris, then turned to modern dance after training in Germany. In 1915, while preparing to perform in London, he collaborated with English composer Gustav Holst on music to accompany his dances. Holst took notes as Itō whistled Japanese folk melodies to him, and those melodies supplied most of the themes of Holst’s Japanese Suite. The following year Itō moved to New York, where he presented his own choreography and advocated for a building in which dancers could perform and rehearse.
items.stem: According to the text, what was Itō’s contribution to Holst’s Japanese Suite?
options: He composed the suite himself and then asked Holst to arrange it for an orchestra.
He created a dance that Holst later set to folk melodies that Holst had collected in Japan.
He performed the suite in New York, where it helped him win support for a new building for dancers.
He provided the folk melodies on which much of the suite’s music was based.
items.explanation: The text says that “Holst took notes as Itō whistled Japanese folk melodies to him, and those melodies supplied most of the themes” of the Japanese Suite. Itō therefore contributed the folk melodies that much of the music was built on.

A.why_wrong: Itō whistled folk melodies and Holst took notes; the text never says Itō composed the suite.

B.why_wrong: The folk melodies came from Itō, who whistled them to Holst; the text never says Holst collected melodies in Japan.

C.why_wrong: Itō did move to New York and advocate for a building for dancers, but the text does not say he performed the suite there or that it helped that effort.

sources.what: Michio Itō (Wikipedia): left Japan as a teenager to study music in Paris, turned to modern dance after Dalcroze training at Hellerau; in 1915 in London Holst took notes while Itō whistled Japanese folk tunes, providing most of the themes of the Japanese Suite, Op. 33; active in New York from 1916, championed a performance space for dancers (Theatre Arts Building)

items.notes: Arts and humanities (dance and music). Distractors recombine the passage's people and places.

items.passage: The Bornean rock frog (Staurois parvus) breeds beside fast-flowing streams whose continuous roar can drown out a frog’s call. Studying the species in Brunei’s Ulu Temburong National Park, T. Ulmar Grafe, Doris Preininger, and colleagues found that males modify the pitch, duration, and repetition rate of their calls so that the calls remain detectable above the noise of the water. Males also wave their conspicuous hind feet in a display called foot flagging, and the researchers’ playback experiments indicated that a call typically precedes a foot flag, alerting other frogs to watch for the display.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The noise of fast-flowing streams keeps Bornean rock frogs from hearing one another’s calls, so the frogs communicate only by foot flagging.
Bornean rock frogs foot-flag more often than other frog species do because their calls are quieter than those of most frogs.
Bornean rock frogs cope with the din of their stream habitat by adjusting their calls and pairing them with a visual display.
Grafe and colleagues found that Bornean rock frogs use foot flagging mainly to attract females that cannot hear the males’ calls.
items.explanation: The text explains that the streams’ “continuous roar can drown out a frog’s call” and then describes two responses: males “modify the pitch, duration, and repetition rate of their calls,” and a call “typically precedes a foot flag.” Choice C sums up both responses to the noisy habitat.

A.why_wrong: The text says males adjust their calls so that the calls “remain detectable above the noise of the water,” so the frogs do not rely only on foot flagging.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares Bornean rock frogs with other frog species, either in how often they foot-flag or in how loud their calls are.

D.why_wrong: The text says calls alert “other frogs” to watch for the foot flag; it never says the display is aimed mainly at females or that females cannot hear the calls.

sources.what: Grafe, Preininger et al. 2012, PLoS One: Staurois parvus at a fast-flowing stream in Ulu Temburong National Park, Brunei; males modified amplitude, pitch, repetition rate and duration of call notes; foot flagging the most conspicuous visual display; playback experiments supported the alerting hypothesis, with advertisement calling preceding foot flagging (PMC3360010)

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Governing claim spread over sentences 1 to 3; key abstracts call changes plus foot flags as 'adjusting their calls and pairing them with a visual display'. Theme overlap: central_ideas_and_details.T6.hard.w4b2_01 (claimed later) is the concave-eared torrent frog, also frogs signalling over stream noise; different species and mechanism.

fixes: kept its subject (Bornean rock frog); CID b2 drops its torrent-frog item

items.passage: Earthquake early warning systems, which can alert people seconds before strong shaking arrives, rely on networks of seismometers that exist in only a few countries. Smartphones, however, are nearly ubiquitous, and each contains an accelerometer, a sensor that detects motion. Qingkai Kong, Richard Allen, and colleagues developed MyShake, an application that uses a phone’s accelerometer to distinguish earthquake shaking from everyday movements and transmits the data to a central system that confirms an earthquake and estimates its location and magnitude. In tests, phones recorded magnitude 5 earthquakes from distances of up to 10 kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Kong and colleagues found that smartphone accelerometers measure earthquakes more accurately than traditional seismometers do.
Researchers have shown that ordinary smartphones could detect earthquakes, which may help extend early warning to places without seismic networks.
MyShake allows people to warn one another about earthquakes by sharing reports of the shaking they personally feel.
Most earthquake early warning systems now depend on smartphones rather than on networks of seismometers.
items.explanation: The text notes that warning systems depend on seismometer networks “that exist in only a few countries,” and then describes MyShake, which uses a phone’s accelerometer to detect earthquake shaking; in tests, phones “recorded magnitude 5 earthquakes.” Choice B joins these points: phones can detect earthquakes and could bring warnings to places that lack seismometers.

A.why_wrong: The text says phones can record earthquakes, but it never compares their accuracy with that of seismometers.

C.why_wrong: MyShake relies on phones’ accelerometers and a central system, not on people reporting what they feel.

D.why_wrong: The text says existing warning systems “rely on networks of seismometers”; MyShake is a new system, not the basis of most current ones.

sources.what: Kong, Allen, Schreier, Kwon 2016, Science Advances, MyShake: EEW systems use networks that exist only in a few nations; smartphones contain accelerometers; on-phone detection separates earthquakes from everyday shakes; central network confirms and estimates location and magnitude; phones record M5 earthquakes at 10 km or less; could provide the only EEW capability in regions without networks (PMC4758737)

items.notes: Technology (seismology, mobile sensing). Key is longest here by design (batch key-longest rate).

items.passage: Most cognitive abilities improve from childhood to adulthood, but Daniel Plebanek and Vladimir Sloutsky identified a case in which young children outperform adults. Four- and five-year-olds and adults viewed sets of shapes after being prompted to attend to particular ones, and then reported whether any of the shapes had changed. Adults were more accurate at detecting changes in the shapes they had been cued to watch, but children were more accurate with the shapes that had not been cued. In a second experiment, the children also remembered more details that were irrelevant to the task they had been given.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Young children notice changes in shapes more accurately than adults do, whether or not they have been told which shapes to watch.
Adults remember fewer details than children do because adults are less willing than children to follow a task’s instructions.
Young children detect changes better than adults do only when they have been told in advance which shapes to watch.
Research suggests that young children attend less selectively than adults do, so they sometimes notice details that adults overlook.
items.explanation: Adults did better with “the shapes they had been cued to watch,” while children did better “with the shapes that had not been cued” and remembered more details “that were irrelevant to the task.” These results show that children spread their attention more widely, which lets them catch what adults miss.

A.why_wrong: Children did better only with the uncued shapes; adults were “more accurate at detecting changes in the shapes they had been cued to watch.”

B.why_wrong: The text never suggests that adults ignore instructions; the adults did well on the shapes they were told to watch.

C.why_wrong: Children outperformed adults on the shapes that “had not been cued,” not on the cued ones.

sources.what: Plebanek and Sloutsky 2017, Psychological Science, Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice What Adults Miss: 4- to 5-year-olds and adults in a change-detection task with cued and uncued shapes; adults better on cued, children better on uncued; children remembered more search-irrelevant features (PMC5461181)

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). Key abstracts the two results into 'attend less selectively'; the paper frames them as a developmental reversal in attention.

items.passage: Pan Yuliang, one of the first Chinese women to paint in the Western style, studied oil painting and figure drawing at academies in Shanghai, Lyon, Paris, and Rome. Yet she did not simply adopt European methods. Her academic training gave her command of oil paint and anatomical accuracy, while Chinese ink painting shaped her emphasis on line, contour, and brushwork. She produced hundreds of ink paintings alongside her oils, and critics praised her for incorporating Chinese ink techniques into Western styles.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Pan joined European and Chinese artistic traditions to develop her own approach to painting.
Pan gave up oil painting in favor of ink painting after she completed her studies in Europe.
Pan was the most widely praised Chinese painter working in Europe during her lifetime.
Pan learned the techniques of Chinese ink painting while studying at academies in Lyon and Rome.
items.explanation: The text says that Pan “did not simply adopt European methods”: her training gave her “command of oil paint and anatomical accuracy,” while “Chinese ink painting shaped her emphasis on line, contour, and brushwork.” Critics also praised her for “incorporating Chinese ink techniques into Western styles.” Choice A sums up this blend.

B.why_wrong: The text says she made ink paintings “alongside her oils,” not that she gave up oil painting.

C.why_wrong: Critics praised her, but the text never ranks her above other Chinese painters in Europe.

D.why_wrong: The text links her European academies to oil painting and figure drawing; it does not say she learned Chinese ink painting there.

sources.what: Pan Yuliang (Wikipedia): first woman in China to paint in the Western style; studied in Shanghai, Lyon, Paris and Rome; hybrid style; European training gave oil painting and anatomical accuracy, Chinese ink painting shaped her emphasis on line, contour and brushwork; known for incorporating Chinese ink techniques into Western styles; Anhui Museum holds 393 of her ink paintings

items.notes: Arts (painting). Profile: aim (beyond European methods), examples (oil, ink), effect (praise). Her early life and nudes left out as needlessly sensitive; the core claim (hybrid style) is what the item tests.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Pierre Loti’s 1886 novel An Iceland Fisherman (translated by Clara Cadiot in 1888). Granny Moan is an elderly woman who lives in a fishing village in Brittany, a region of France.

With great care and good management she managed to appear pretty well dressed, although her gowns were much darned, and hardly held together. She always wore the tiny brown Paimpol shawl, which was for best, and upon which the long muslin rolls of her white caps had fallen for past sixty years.

She still carried herself very straight, not at all like an old woman; and, in spite of her pointed chin, her soft eyes and delicate profile made all think her still very charming. She was held in great respect—one could see that if only by the nods that people gave her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Granny Moan is embarrassed by her worn clothing and tries to avoid being seen by her neighbors.
Granny Moan has grown frail with age, although her neighbors still greet her kindly.
Though her clothes are old and mended, Granny Moan keeps a dignified appearance and is respected by others.
Granny Moan is admired in the village mainly because she can afford to dress more finely than her neighbors can.
items.explanation: The text says Granny Moan’s “gowns were much darned,” yet “With great care and good management she managed to appear pretty well dressed.” She “carried herself very straight” and “was held in great respect.” Choice C combines her worn clothes, her dignified bearing, and the respect she receives.

A.why_wrong: Granny Moan takes care to look well dressed and carries herself “very straight”; nothing suggests embarrassment or hiding, and people greet her with nods.

B.why_wrong: People do greet her with nods, but she is not frail: she “carried herself very straight, not at all like an old woman.”

D.why_wrong: Her gowns “were much darned, and hardly held together,” so she is not wealthier or more finely dressed than others; the respect she receives is not tied to money.

Loti, An Iceland Fisherman, translated by Clara Cadiot (New York: Gottsberger, 1888), title page and text matching Gutenberg #2196 word for word

items.passage: Khoa Reef is a submerged ridge in Lake Titicaca, near the northwestern tip of Bolivia’s Island of the Sun. There, archaeologists Christophe Delaere, José Capriles, and colleagues conducted the first systematic underwater excavations at the site, recovering objects deposited by people of the Tiwanaku state, which flourished around the lake between the fifth and twelfth centuries CE. The finds included ceramic incense burners shaped like felines, the bones of young llamas, and ornaments of gold and shell, and scattered among these offerings were several stone anchors.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can be concluded about the Tiwanaku offerings at Khoa Reef?
options: They were likely placed in the lake by people working from boats.
They were likely meant to be retrieved later, since they included gold ornaments.
They were likely left there by visitors from outside the Tiwanaku state.
They were likely intended to mark a safe route for boats crossing the lake.
items.explanation: The offerings lie on a “submerged ridge,” and “scattered among these offerings were several stone anchors,” which are used to hold boats in place. Together these details suggest that the offerings were dropped into the lake from boats.

B.why_wrong: The text lists gold ornaments among the offerings but gives no sign that anyone planned to recover them.

C.why_wrong: The text says the objects were “deposited by people of the Tiwanaku state.”

D.why_wrong: The anchors suggest that boats stopped at the reef, not that the offerings marked a route; the text calls the objects offerings.

sources.what: Delaere, Capriles, Stanish 2019, PNAS, Underwater ritual offerings in the Island of the Sun and the formation of the Tiwanaku state: first systematic underwater excavations at Khoa Reef; ceramic feline incense burners, juvenile llamas, metal, shell and lapidary ornaments; offerings likely deposited during rituals held from boats, as suggested by the presence of andesite anchors (PMC6486741)

items.notes: Archaeology. P1: offerings on a submerged reef; P2: stone anchors among them; unstated conclusion (the authors' own): deposited from boats. Different subject from the Uros reed islands and waru waru items set at Lake Titicaca.

items.passage: Germaine Tailleferre first gained renown in Paris as the only woman in Les Six, a group of young composers who achieved sudden fame after the critic Henri Collet wrote about them. Membership in the group, however, accounts for only a small part of her career. Tailleferre continued composing until a few weeks before her death in 1983 at age ninety-one, producing concertos, operas, ballets, and more than thirty film scores, and most of the music she wrote after 1946 was not published until after she died.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Tailleferre wrote most of her important works while she belonged to Les Six and composed little once the group’s fame faded.
Although Tailleferre first became known as a member of Les Six, her work as a composer continued for decades beyond the group’s early fame.
Tailleferre became famous in Paris only after the music she wrote after 1946 was published following her death.
Tailleferre eventually left Les Six because the group’s other members did not take her music seriously.
items.explanation: The text says Tailleferre “first gained renown in Paris as the only woman in Les Six” but that the group “accounts for only a small part of her career,” since she “continued composing until a few weeks before her death in 1983.” Choice B states this contrast.

A.why_wrong: The text says she kept composing for decades, producing concertos, operas, ballets, and film scores, so she did not stop composing after the group’s early fame.

C.why_wrong: She gained renown in Paris through Les Six; the posthumous publication of her later music came long after she was already known.

D.why_wrong: The text never says she left the group or that its members dismissed her music.

items.notes: Arts (music). View then correction: the Les Six label versus a sixty-year career. 'Accounts for only a small part of her career' is the passage's own evaluative framing, supported by the dated facts that follow.

items.passage: In the early 1960s, the rising waters of Lake Nasser, a newly created reservoir, threatened to submerge the ancient settlement of Faras on the border between Egypt and Sudan. From 1960 to 1964, a Polish expedition directed by archaeologist Kazimierz Michałowski excavated the site. Inside a hill, the team discovered a cathedral that had been completely filled with sand. Because of the sand, the cathedral’s wall paintings of saints, bishops, and kings were well preserved. The archaeologists removed 120 of the paintings before the site was flooded, and many are now exhibited in museums in Warsaw and Khartoum.
items.stem: According to the text, why were the wall paintings in the cathedral at Faras well preserved?
options: Michałowski’s team covered them before the town was flooded.
They had been created by artists from Warsaw and Khartoum.
The waters of Lake Nasser kept them cool for many years.
The sand that filled the cathedral protected them.
items.explanation: The text says the team found “a cathedral that had been completely filled with sand” and that “Because of the sand, the cathedral’s wall paintings of saints, bishops, and kings were well preserved.”

A.why_wrong: The team removed paintings before the flood; the text never says they covered the paintings, and the paintings were already well preserved when found.

B.why_wrong: Warsaw and Khartoum are where many paintings are exhibited today, not where the painters came from.

C.why_wrong: The paintings were removed before the site was flooded, so the lake’s water did not preserve them; the sand did.

sources.what: Faras (Wikipedia): flooded by Lake Nasser in the 1960s; Polish team led by Kazimierz Michałowski excavated 1960 to 1964; a hill concealed a cathedral completely filled with sand, which kept its structure and paintings well preserved; paintings of archangels, monarchs, bishops, saints; 120 of 169 paintings removed; displayed in Warsaw and Khartoum

items.notes: Archaeology. 'Kings' renders the source's 'monarchs'.

items.passage: Many newborns experience respiratory distress, and physicians in wealthy countries frequently treat them with bubble CPAP, a device that delivers a continuous flow of pressurized air to keep an infant’s lungs open. Most hospitals in low-income countries have not used these devices because they are too expensive. A team that included bioengineers at Rice University in Texas designed a version that costs about fifteen times less. When physicians tested it in Blantyre, Malawi, 71 percent of the infants who received it survived, compared with 44 percent of those given oxygen through the nose.
items.stem: According to the text, what did physicians in Blantyre, Malawi, find when they tested the new device?
options: It cost about fifteen times more than the devices used in wealthy countries.
It was easier for nurses to use than the devices used in wealthy countries.
More of the infants who received it survived than infants given oxygen through the nose.
It helped infants breathe more easily but did not change how many of them survived.
items.explanation: The text says that “71 percent of the infants who received it survived, compared with 44 percent of those given oxygen through the nose.”

A.why_wrong: The new version “costs about fifteen times less,” not more.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how easy the device was for nurses to operate.

D.why_wrong: Survival did change: 71 percent of infants who received the device survived, compared with 44 percent of the others.

sources.what: Kawaza et al., Efficacy of a low-cost bubble CPAP system in treatment of respiratory distress in a neonatal ward in Malawi: cost of existing CPAP prohibitive in low-resource settings; new system about $350, a fifteen-fold cost reduction; Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Blantyre; survival 71.0% with bCPAP vs 44.0% with nasal oxygen; authors from Rice University bioengineering (PMC5117003)

items.notes: Technology (medical devices). The study also had Baylor and University of Malawi authors, hence 'a team that included bioengineers at Rice'. 'To keep an infant's lungs open' is the standard description of CPAP, not a study finding.

items.passage: In 2006, Jane Wiggins photographed an unusual undulating layer of clouds from an office window in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and submitted the image to the Cloud Appreciation Society, which displayed it in its online gallery. Over the following years, people submitted many photographs of similar formations to the society. Gavin Pretor-Pinney, the society’s founder, then collaborated with the Royal Meteorological Society to have the clouds officially recognized as a new type. In 2017, the formation was added to the International Cloud Atlas under the name asperitas, the first addition since 1951.
items.stem: According to the text, what helped lead to the recognition of asperitas clouds?
options: Members of the public sent many photographs of the clouds to the Cloud Appreciation Society.
Scientists in Iowa measured the height of the clouds from an office building in Cedar Rapids.
Pretor-Pinney photographed the clouds himself while he was visiting Cedar Rapids in 2006.
The International Cloud Atlas had asked the public to look for new cloud types in 2006.
items.explanation: The text says that Wiggins sent her image to the Cloud Appreciation Society and that “people submitted many photographs of similar formations to the society,” after which Pretor-Pinney worked to have the clouds “officially recognized as a new type.”

B.why_wrong: The office window in Cedar Rapids is where Wiggins took her photograph; the text mentions no scientists measuring the clouds there.

C.why_wrong: Jane Wiggins, not Pretor-Pinney, photographed the clouds in Cedar Rapids in 2006.

D.why_wrong: The text never says the Cloud Atlas asked the public for help; the photos went to the Cloud Appreciation Society.

sources.what: Asperitas (cloud) (Wikipedia): Jane Wiggins photographed it from an office window in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 2006 and sent it to the Cloud Appreciation Society, which displayed it; many similar photos followed; Gavin Pretor-Pinney worked with the Royal Meteorological Society to promote it; added to the WMO International Cloud Atlas in 2017, the first formation added since 1951

items.notes: Natural science (meteorology, citizen science). The Atlas lists asperitas as a 'supplementary feature'; the passage says 'cloud formation', as the source does.

items.passage: Many plants have sharp spines, which scientists have long thought mainly protect plants from large plant-eating mammals. Rupesh Kariyat and his team tested whether spines also defend plants against caterpillars. When the researchers removed the spines from some horsenettle plants, caterpillars reached the leaves much more quickly than they did on plants that still had their spines. On plant species with more spines, the caterpillars also took longer to eat all of the leaves.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research shows that caterpillars refuse to eat the leaves of plants that have spines.
Research suggests that spines can protect plants from caterpillars by slowing them down.
Researchers found that spines harm large mammals more than they harm caterpillars.
Researchers found that horsenettle plants grow more spines after mammals feed on them.
items.explanation: The text reports that without spines, “caterpillars reached the leaves much more quickly,” and that on plants with more spines, “the caterpillars also took longer to eat all of the leaves.” So the research suggests that spines protect plants from caterpillars by slowing them down.

A.why_wrong: The caterpillars still ate the leaves of spiny plants; they just “took longer” to do so.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how much spines harm mammals with how much they harm caterpillars.

D.why_wrong: The researchers removed spines to test caterpillars; the text says nothing about spines growing after mammals feed.

sources.what: Kariyat, Hardison, De Moraes, Mescher 2017, Biology Letters, Plant spines deter herbivory by restricting caterpillar movement: spines thought to function primarily against mammalian herbivores; Manduca sexta caterpillars located leaves much more quickly on plants with spines removed; took longer to defoliate species with more spines (PMC5454246)

items.notes: Natural science (plant defense). Caterpillar species (tobacco hornworm) left unnamed: our CID w3b1_01 already uses hornworm larvae for a different study.

items.passage: Today most people smile when they are photographed, but that was not always the custom. Shiry Ginosar and her colleagues developed a computer program to measure the smiles in more than 37,000 portraits from American high school yearbooks, photographed over approximately a century. The analysis revealed that smiles became increasingly common and broader from the 1900s to the 1950s, a trend that has continued since then. It also revealed that, on average, women smiled more than men did.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that high school students in the early 1900s were less happy than students are today.
A computer program showed that men smiled more than women did in early yearbook photos.
Yearbook photographers began requiring students to smile for their portraits in the 1950s.
An analysis of yearbook portraits found that smiling for photographs grew more widespread over the twentieth century.
items.explanation: The text says the analysis found that “smiles became increasingly common and broader from the 1900s to the 1950s, a trend that has continued since then.” Choice D states this finding about yearbook portraits.

A.why_wrong: The study measured smiles in portraits; the text says nothing about how happy the students were.

B.why_wrong: The text says that “women smiled more than men did.”

C.why_wrong: The text never explains why smiles increased or mentions rules set by photographers.

sources.what: Ginosar, Rakelly, Sachs, Yin, Lee, Krähenbühl, Efros 2015, A Century of Portraits: A Visual Historical Record of American High School Yearbooks (37,921 frontal portraits); lip-curvature smile metric shows a rapid increase in smile popularity and intensity from the 1900s to the 1950s, a trend that still continues; women consistently smile more than men (section on smiling in portraiture)

items.notes: Social science (history of photography and social norms). Finding sits in the paper body, not the abstract; the PDF URL states it.

items.passage: In 1895, Zaida Ben-Yusuf emigrated from England to the United States, settling in New York, where she worked as a milliner, or hat maker. Within two years, she had opened her own portrait studio on Fifth Avenue. There she made artistic portraits of wealthy, fashionable, and famous Americans. Her portraits appeared in exhibitions in London, Paris, and Glasgow, and in 1901 a magazine named her one of the foremost women photographers in America. She also wrote magazine articles that explained her methods to amateur photographers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Ben-Yusuf gave up photography so that she could return to making hats for wealthy customers.
Ben-Yusuf mostly photographed the hats that she designed for customers in New York.
Ben-Yusuf became a successful portrait photographer whose work was exhibited and praised in several countries.
Ben-Yusuf was the first woman to open a portrait photography studio in New York.
items.explanation: The text says Ben-Yusuf opened “her own portrait studio on Fifth Avenue,” that her portraits “appeared in exhibitions in London, Paris, and Glasgow,” and that a magazine named her “one of the foremost women photographers in America.” Choice C sums up this success.

A.why_wrong: The text describes her moving from hat making to photography, not back again.

B.why_wrong: She made hats before opening her studio, but the text says she made portraits of “wealthy, fashionable, and famous Americans,” not pictures of hats.

D.why_wrong: The text calls her one of the foremost women photographers, but it never says she was the first woman to open a studio.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Richard Jefferies’s 1882 novel Bevis: The Story of a Boy. Bevis, a boy who lives on a farm in England, has been trying to build a boat from wooden planks.

Pan, the spaniel, sat down on the hard, dry, beaten earth of the workshop, and looked at Bevis puzzling over his plane and his pencil, his footrule, and the paper on which he had sketched his model; then up at Bevis’s forehead, frowning over the trouble of it. No. This would not do; Bevis could not wait long enough; Bevis liked the sunshine and the grass under foot. Crash fell the plank and bang went the hammer as he flung it on the bench, and away they tore out into the field.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Bevis wants to finish the boat quickly so that he can take Pan out on the water.
Bevis abandons a frustrating task because he would rather be outdoors.
Bevis grows angry with Pan for distracting him while he works on the boat.
Bevis finishes sketching a model of his boat and goes outside to show it to Pan.
items.explanation: Bevis is “frowning over the trouble of” building the boat. Then the text says “This would not do; Bevis could not wait long enough; Bevis liked the sunshine and the grass under foot,” and he throws down his tools and runs into the field. He gives up the hard task because he would rather be outside.

A.why_wrong: The text never says why Bevis wants a boat, and he does not hurry to finish it; he stops working.

C.why_wrong: Pan only sits and watches, and the two run off together happily; Bevis is frustrated by the work, not angry with Pan.

D.why_wrong: Bevis “flung” his tools down without finishing; he goes outside to enjoy “the sunshine and the grass,” not to show Pan a sketch.

sources.what: Richard Jefferies, Bevis: The Story of a Boy (Project Gutenberg #35930), chapter I

items.notes: Literary prose. Adapted from Gutenberg #35930: 'Pan: the spaniel' corrected to 'Pan, the spaniel'; the clause about Pan biting fleas cut and the sentence closed after 'trouble of it'; the final sentence trimmed after 'out into the field'. Context line replaces the preceding paragraphs about the planks.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Eleanor Gates’s 1912 novel The Poor Little Rich Girl. Gwendolyn, a young girl, is looking into a pier glass, a tall mirror.

Halfway up the shining surface of the gilt-framed pier glass was a mark—a tiny ink-line that had been carefully drawn across the outer edge of the wide bevel. She had drawn the tiny line across the edge of the bevel the evening before, when she was only six years old; now it was mid-morning of another day, and she was seven—yet she was not a whit taller! The tears began to overflow.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Gwendolyn most likely feel when she looks at the mark on the mirror?
options: She feels disappointed because she expected to be taller now that she is seven.
She feels frightened because someone has drawn a strange mark on her mirror.
She feels proud because she has grown since she drew the line the evening before.
She feels annoyed because she has to stop playing to measure her height.
items.explanation: Gwendolyn drew the line “when she was only six years old,” and now, on the morning after, she is seven, yet “she was not a whit taller!” Then “The tears began to overflow.” She is disappointed because she expected her birthday to make her taller.

B.why_wrong: Gwendolyn drew the mark herself “the evening before,” so it is not a strange mark made by someone else.

C.why_wrong: The text says “she was not a whit taller,” and she begins to cry, so she has not grown and is not proud.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests she was interrupted while playing; she measures herself on purpose and cries at the result.

sources.what: Eleanor Gates, The Poor Little Rich Girl (Project Gutenberg #15714), chapter I

items.notes: Literary prose (feeling plus reason, as in 1.15). Adapted from Gutenberg #15714: three sentences kept (opening, the line drawn the evening before, the tears), the sentences between them cut; double hyphens set as closed em dashes; italics on 'yet she was not a whit taller!' dropped. Context line glosses pier glass.
