items.passage: Decision theorists generally treat a rational choice as one that best satisfies the values a person already holds. That framework struggles with someone who enrolls in a music course hoping to come to love music she does not yet appreciate: if her existing values already favor the undertaking, she has nothing to acquire; if they do not, the undertaking appears irrational. In Aspiration (2018), philosopher Agnes Callard argues that such a person acts on “proleptic reasons,” which anticipate a value the person grasps only partially, so that the effort to acquire new values can itself be rational.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Callard holds that a person working to appreciate something new is guided by the values she already has, which is what makes the effort rational.
Callard argues that decision theory, once expanded to include proleptic reasons, can explain how people come to value things they once did not.
Callard contends that a person who hopes to come to love an activity acts rationally only if that hope is eventually realized.
Callard maintains that a person can be rational in trying to come to value something whose worth she only partly sees.
items.explanation: The text sets out a puzzle: someone trying to come to love music seems either to have “nothing to acquire” or to be acting irrationally. Callard’s answer is that such a person acts on reasons that “anticipate a value the person grasps only partially,” so that “the effort to acquire new values can itself be rational.” Choice D states that claim.

A.recipe: twisted detail (current values for anticipated ones)
A.why_wrong: Being guided by values she already has is the horn of the puzzle that leaves her “nothing to acquire”; Callard’s reasons anticipate a value grasped only partially.

B.recipe: plausible but unsupported (invented relation to the old view)
B.why_wrong: The text presents proleptic reasons as Callard’s answer to a case that decision theory’s framework “struggles with”; it never says she expands decision theory.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text makes the rationality of the effort depend on whether the person eventually comes to love the activity.

sources.what: Agnes Callard, Aspiration: The Agency of Becoming (2018): aspiration is rational agency aimed at acquiring values, not understandable in terms of decision theory; aspirants act on 'proleptic reasons' and are guided by the values of the self they aspire to be, with an imperfect grasp of those values

items.notes: Humanities (philosophy), scholar-argument passage like 3.20. The music-course case is the passage's own illustration, not attributed to Callard. Distractors: current-values twist, invented revision of decision theory, invented success condition.

fixes: key D paraphrased away from the passage (was 'act rationally in striving to acquire a value that she does not yet fully grasp', echoing 'acquire', 'value', 'grasps'); same claim; re-solved blind, D only
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed (Wikipedia, Aspiration section: aspiration is rational agency aimed at acquiring values, cannot be understood in terms of decision theory, proleptic reasons, imperfect grasp). Fame judged acceptable: Callard is a known public philosopher, but the proleptic-reasons argument is not a pop topic a student would recognize, and no option can be chosen from outside knowledge.

band7.why: Scholar argument: puzzle then answer. B (decision theory expanded) is a close attribution-style trap, A twists current values, C adds a condition. Key now paraphrased. Band 6, as planned.

items.passage: For about 150 years, astronomers have described many of the star-forming gas clouds near the Sun as components of the Gould Belt, an expanding ring of young stars, gas, and dust tilted roughly 20 degrees to the plane of the Milky Way. Yet distances to these clouds were measured too imprecisely to reveal their actual three-dimensional arrangement. Using newly precise measurements, João Alves et al. mapped the clouds and found that many lie along a narrow, undulating filament of gas about 9,000 light-years long, a configuration inconsistent with a ring.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Gas clouds near the Sun have long been thought to form a ring, but a new map suggests that they are arranged quite differently.
Measurements by Alves et al. indicate that the Gould Belt is a far longer ring than astronomers had believed, stretching some 9,000 light-years.
Although many clouds near the Sun lie along a wavelike band, that band likely formed when an earlier ring of young stars and gas broke apart.
Astronomers had long doubted that the clouds near the Sun form a ring, and the precise distances measured by Alves et al. have confirmed those doubts.
items.explanation: For about 150 years astronomers have treated many nearby gas clouds as “components of the Gould Belt,” a ring. Alves et al.’s map shows many of those clouds lying along “a narrow, undulating filament of gas,” a configuration “inconsistent with a ring.” Choice A captures both the long-held view and its revision.

B.why_wrong: The 9,000 light-year figure describes the undulating filament Alves et al. found, which the text calls “inconsistent with a ring,” not a longer Gould Belt.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how the band formed or about an earlier ring breaking apart.

D.why_wrong: Astronomers did not doubt the ring; they described the clouds as components of the Gould Belt for about 150 years. Only the clouds’ distances were measured too imprecisely.

sources.what: Alves et al. 2020, Nature: for 150 years the local interstellar medium was viewed through the Gould Belt, an expanding ring tilted about 20 degrees to the Galactic plane; distance errors hid the clouds' arrangement; a 2.7-kiloparsec narrow undulating structure contains many Gould Belt clouds and is inconsistent with a ring

items.notes: Natural science (astronomy). View then correction; key holds both halves. 2.7 kpc is about 8,800 light-years, rounded to 'about 9,000'. Distractors: ring kept and lengthened, invented origin, old view misstated as doubt.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the Nature abstract (PubMed 31910431): 150-year Gould Belt view, distance errors, 2.7-kpc undulating structure inconsistent with a ring. The passage never names the Radcliffe Wave; fame judged acceptable.

band7.why: View then correction signalled by a plain 'Yet', not a stance word, so band 6. B and D twist the old view, C keeps the true band and invents an origin.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Frances Cornford’s 1915 poem “People.” A watering place is a seaside resort, and fastnesses are remote, well-protected strongholds.

Like to islands in the seas,
Stand our personalities—
Islands where we always face
One another’s watering place.
When we promenade our sands
We can hear each other’s bands,
We can see on festal nights
Red and green and purple lights,
Gilt pavilions in a row,
Stucco houses built for show.

But our eyes can never reach
Further than the foolish beach,
Never can they hope to win
To the fastnesses within.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: People devote so much effort to impressive displays for others that they neglect to develop their own inner lives.
People can perceive only the surface of one another’s characters, never the depths that lie beneath it.
People who live near one another, like neighboring islanders, come to know each other well through shared celebrations.
People deliberately hide their true selves behind cheerful displays because they fear how others would judge them.
items.explanation: The speaker compares “our personalities” to “islands” that face one another: we can “hear each other’s bands” and see “Stucco houses built for show,” but “our eyes can never reach / Further than the foolish beach” and cannot reach “the fastnesses within.” The poem’s point is that people see only the outward show of one another’s characters, never what lies deeper.

A.recipe: plausible but unsupported (moral read into an image)
A.why_wrong: The houses are “built for show,” but the poem never says that people neglect their inner lives; it says others cannot see those inner places.

C.why_wrong: The islanders see each other’s festivities, yet their “eyes can never reach / Further than the foolish beach,” so they do not come to know each other well.

D.why_wrong: The poem says others’ eyes cannot reach the inner places, not that people hide themselves on purpose or out of fear of judgment.

sources.what: Frances Cornford, 'People', in Spring Morning (Poetry Bookshop, 1915); 1915 edition scan confirms the poem and its text
Project Gutenberg text of Spring Morning (1923 edition)

items.notes: Poem, extended metaphor like 3.17. Adapted: first 14 of 20 lines; final colon changed to a period. Glosses for watering place and fastnesses. 72 words. Distractors: moral of vanity, literal neighborly reading, invented motive of fear.

fixes: restored the stanza break before 'But our eyes can never reach' (1915 Poetry Bookshop edition and Gutenberg 60396 both set it)
review.facts_note: Text checked against the archive.org scan of Spring Morning (Poetry Bookshop, a 1918 second-thousand printing of the 1915 collection) and Gutenberg 60396: first 14 lines exact, final colon set as a period.

band7.why: Poem with one extended figure carried to a general claim; distractors are two UNS and one LIT, a band-6 shape. Band 6, as planned.

items.passage: In 1774 Mary Katharine Goddard assumed control of the Maryland Journal, a Baltimore newspaper established by her brother, and she continued publishing it throughout the Revolutionary War while also serving as the city’s postmaster. In January 1777, when the Continental Congress ordered that the Declaration of Independence be distributed widely, Goddard volunteered her press. Previously printed copies had displayed only two names, those of John Hancock and Charles Thomson, but her edition, now known as the Goddard Broadside, was the first to include the names of the signatories.
items.stem: According to the text, how did the Goddard Broadside differ from earlier printed copies of the Declaration of Independence?
options: It was the first copy that Congress ordered to be widely distributed.
It was printed on the press that Goddard’s brother had used for his newspaper.
It left out the names of John Hancock and Charles Thomson.
It listed the names of the people who had signed the Declaration.
items.explanation: The text says that previously printed copies “had displayed only two names” but that the Goddard Broadside “was the first to include the names of the signatories.” So it differed from earlier copies by listing the people who signed the Declaration.

A.why_wrong: Congress’s order concerned distributing the Declaration in general; the text never says Goddard’s was the first copy Congress ordered.

B.why_wrong: The text says Goddard “volunteered her press” and that her brother established the newspaper, but it never says the broadside was printed on a press he had used.

C.why_wrong: Hancock and Thomson were the two names on earlier copies; nothing suggests Goddard left them off a broadside that included the signers’ names.

sources.what: Mary Katharine Goddard: took over the Maryland Journal in 1774, Baltimore postmaster from 1775; offered her press after Congress's January 1777 order; the Goddard Broadside was the first copy with the typeset names of the signers, earlier copies naming only Hancock and Thomson; her name printed at the bottom

items.notes: History. Explicit detail across two sentences (earlier copies vs hers). Distractors: twisted order, recombined press, reversed names.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia: earlier printings named only Hancock and Thomson; the Goddard Broadside first included the signers' names; she offered her press after the January 1777 order.

items.passage: Julia Morgan, the first woman admitted to the architecture program of Paris’s École des Beaux-Arts, became in 1904 the first woman licensed as an architect in California. That same year she completed her first structure of reinforced concrete, El Campanil, a 72-foot bell tower at Mills College in Oakland, although some of her colleagues doubted her expertise with the material. Two years later, the 1906 San Francisco earthquake left the tower unscathed. Its survival built Morgan’s reputation, and over her career she went on to design some 800 buildings.
items.stem: According to the text, what helped establish Morgan’s reputation as an architect?
options: A tower she designed came through a major earthquake without damage.
She trained in Paris, where few American architects had been able to study.
Her colleagues praised the bell tower she built at Mills College.
She was the first architect in California to build with reinforced concrete.
items.explanation: The text says the 1906 earthquake “left the tower unscathed” and that “Its survival built Morgan’s reputation.” So the tower’s coming through the earthquake undamaged is what helped establish her reputation.

B.why_wrong: Morgan did study in Paris, but the text never says how many American architects studied there or credits her training with building her reputation.

C.why_wrong: The text says “some of her colleagues doubted her expertise,” not that they praised the tower.

D.why_wrong: El Campanil was Morgan’s own “first structure of reinforced concrete”; the text does not say she was the first architect in California to use the material.

sources.what: Julia Morgan: first woman admitted to architecture at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and first woman licensed as an architect in California (1904); El Campanil, 72-foot bell tower at Mills College, her first reinforced concrete structure (1904); unscathed in the 1906 earthquake, which built her reputation; colleagues doubted her concrete expertise; about 800 buildings

items.notes: Arts (architecture). Explicit detail with a light paraphrase (unscathed, without damage).

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia: El Campanil survived the 1906 earthquake unscathed, which helped build Morgan's reputation.

items.passage: In 1891 New Zealand suffragist Kate Sheppard organized a petition to Parliament, signed by approximately 10,000 women, supporting legislation that would allow women to vote; the bill passed one chamber but was defeated in the other. Sheppard promised that her next petition would be twice as large, and in 1892 it gathered more than 20,000 signatures, yet that year’s bill also failed. Her third petition, presented in 1893, contained nearly 32,000 signatures, the largest Parliament had yet received. Later that year, legislation granting women the vote was finally enacted.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the petitions that Sheppard organized?
options: Each one led Parliament to enact legislation allowing women to vote.
The first one failed because it had too few signatures to be considered.
Each one was signed by more people than the one before it.
The last one was presented after women had already been granted the vote.
items.explanation: The petitions grew each time: the first was “signed by approximately 10,000 women,” the second “gathered more than 20,000 signatures,” and the third “contained nearly 32,000 signatures.” So each petition had more signers than the one before.

A.why_wrong: The bills of 1891 and 1892 both failed; only “Later that year,” after the third petition, was legislation enacted.

B.why_wrong: The 1891 bill “passed one chamber but was defeated in the other”; the text gives no sign that the petition was too small to be considered.

D.why_wrong: The third petition was presented in 1893, and legislation granting women the vote was enacted “Later that year.”

sources.what: Kate Sheppard: petitions of 1891 (10,085 signatures), 1892 (20,274) and 1893 (31,872, the largest petition presented to Parliament at that point); 1891 and 1892 bills failed; women's suffrage law passed in 1893

items.notes: History. Detail drawn from three sentences (the three counts). Figures rounded (10,085 about 10,000; 31,872 nearly 32,000).

fixes: 'submitted' changed to 'organized' (John Hall presented the 1891 petition to Parliament; Sheppard organized it)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia: 10,085, 20,274 and 31,872 signatures; 1891 and 1892 bills failed; suffrage enacted 1893.

items.passage: Returning astronauts from Mars would require a rocket fueled partly by tens of tons of oxygen, and transporting that oxygen from Earth would mean launching hundreds of tons of material. MOXIE, an instrument aboard NASA’s Perseverance rover, investigates an alternative: it uses electricity to split carbon dioxide, the predominant gas in the Martian atmosphere, and release oxygen. Jeffrey Hoffman, Michael Hecht, and colleagues reported that MOXIE produced oxygen seven times during 2021, and they argue that a larger version could eventually manufacture the necessary oxygen on Mars itself.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: MOXIE has already produced enough oxygen on Mars to fuel a rocket carrying astronauts back to Earth.
An experiment on Mars suggests that oxygen for future missions might be made from the planet’s own atmosphere.
Because carbon dioxide is scarce on Mars, MOXIE depends on supplies of the gas shipped from Earth.
Researchers have found that making oxygen on Mars would cost more than launching it from Earth.
items.explanation: MOXIE splits “carbon dioxide, the predominant gas in the Martian atmosphere,” to release oxygen, and it “produced oxygen seven times during 2021.” Its developers argue that “a larger version could eventually manufacture the necessary oxygen on Mars itself.” Choice B joins the result and its implication.

A.why_wrong: MOXIE produced oxygen seven times as a test; only “a larger version” might one day make the tens of tons a rocket would need.

C.why_wrong: The text calls carbon dioxide “the predominant gas in the Martian atmosphere,” and MOXIE uses that gas; nothing is shipped from Earth.

D.why_wrong: The text presents making oxygen on Mars as a way to avoid launching “hundreds of tons of material,” not as the costlier choice.

sources.what: Hoffman, Hecht et al. 2022, Science Advances: MOXIE produces oxygen by solid oxide electrolysis of atmospheric CO2; a scaled-up MOXIE could make on site the tens of tons of oxygen a rocket needs instead of launching hundreds of tons from Earth; produced oxygen seven times between landing in February 2021 and the end of 2021

items.notes: Technology. Study report: problem, device and method, result, implication; key joins result and implication with the passage's hedge.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the Science Advances abstract (PMC9432831).

items.passage: Trees are typically regarded as separate individuals, but the roots of neighboring trees of the same species frequently fuse, forming natural grafts. Martin Bader and Sebastian Leuzinger examined a leafless kauri stump in a New Zealand forest that had remained alive despite being unable to photosynthesize, measuring water movement in the stump and in surrounding kauri trees. The stump’s water levels declined during the day, when its neighbors were drawing up the most water, and recovered at night, when they drew up little. The researchers propose that trees connected this way may share a “communal physiology.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Kauri stumps store water during the day and pass it on to neighboring trees at night, when those trees need it most.
Kauri trees whose roots have fused with a stump grow more slowly because they must share their water with it.
Research on a kauri stump suggests that trees joined by their roots may work together rather than as fully separate individuals.
Because the kauri stump had no leaves, it took in most of its water directly from the soil rather than through its neighbors.
items.explanation: Although trees are “typically regarded as separate individuals,” the stump’s water levels rose and fell in step with its neighbors’ water use, and the researchers propose that connected trees “may share a ‘communal physiology.’” Choice C states this finding at the passage’s level of certainty.

A.why_wrong: The timing is reversed: the stump’s water levels declined by day, when its neighbors drew up the most water, and recovered at night, so the stump depends on its neighbors rather than storing water and passing it on to them.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how fast the neighboring trees grow.

D.why_wrong: The stump’s water levels tracked its neighbors’ water use, which points to a link through fused roots, not to independent uptake from the soil.

sources.what: Bader and Leuzinger 2019, iScience: leafless kauri (Agathis australis) stump kept alive by conspecific neighbors through root grafts; stump water potential low by day and high at night, coinciding with peak and minimal sap flow in neighbors; suggests a 'communal physiology' among trees

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). 'Water levels' simplifies stem water potential. Key paraphrases the governing claim with the researchers' hedge.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the iScience abstract (PMC6831820).

items.passage: In the late 1920s at Vienna’s Social and Economic Museum, director Otto Neurath set out to make statistics about the city comprehensible to ordinary visitors, schoolchildren included. Collaborating with illustrator Gerd Arntz and with Marie Reidemeister, who transformed complex data into preliminary sketches for charts, he developed a pictorial method later called Isotype. Its charts employed simple symbols that each represented a fixed quantity: a larger amount was indicated not by an enlarged symbol but by additional copies of the same one, so that viewers could compare quantities at a glance and even count them.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Neurath and his collaborators created a way of presenting data in pictures so that the general public could understand it.
Neurath hired Arntz mainly to produce artworks depicting the daily lives of the people who lived in Vienna.
Isotype charts were widely praised by professional statisticians for being more precise than tables of numbers.
Neurath’s charts became steadily more abstract over the years as the museum’s exhibitions began to travel abroad.
items.explanation: Neurath wanted “to make statistics about the city comprehensible to ordinary visitors,” and with Arntz and Reidemeister he developed “a pictorial method” whose repeated symbols let viewers “compare quantities at a glance.” Choice A sums up the aim and the method.

B.recipe: one example presented as the purpose (twisted)
B.why_wrong: Arntz worked on the charts as an illustrator within the method; the text never says he was hired to make artworks about daily life.

C.why_wrong: The text does not mention statisticians’ opinions or compare the charts’ precision with that of tables.

D.recipe: chronological story the text does not tell
D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the charts changing over time or about exhibitions abroad.

sources.what: Isotype: developed at Vienna's Social and Economic Museum 1925-1934 under director Otto Neurath to represent social facts pictorially for ordinary citizens including schoolchildren; Gerd Arntz made the graphics (in Vienna from 1929); Marie Reidemeister transformed data into chart sketches; larger quantities shown by more same-sized pictograms, which can be counted

items.notes: Arts and humanities (design). Profile of a method: aim, collaborators, rule, effect. Distractors per T3 recipe: example as purpose, invented reputation, invented chronology.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia (Isotype): Vienna Social and Economic Museum, Neurath, Arntz, Reidemeister as transformer, ordinary citizens including schoolchildren.

items.passage:
The following text is from Stella Benson’s 1917 novel This Is the End. Cousin Gustus, a man in his late sixties, raised his young relatives Jay and Kew from childhood.

Cousin Gustus is an expert pessimist. Vice, accidents, and terrible ends are his speciality. All virtue is to him an exception, and by him is immediately forgotten. In sudden deaths you cannot catch him out. If you were tossed from the horns of a bull into the jaws of a crocodile, and died of pneumonia contracted during the flight, you would not surprise Cousin Gustus. He is never at a loss for a precedent. The only way you could really astonish him would be by living a blameless life without adventure, and dying of old age in your bed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Cousin Gustus enjoys telling exaggerated stories about the dangerous adventures he has survived.
Cousin Gustus is so fearful of accidents and sudden deaths that he avoids anything that might be risky.
Cousin Gustus believes that people who live quiet, careful lives deserve the most admiration.
Cousin Gustus so firmly expects misfortune that only a quiet, ordinary life would surprise him.
items.explanation: Cousin Gustus is “an expert pessimist” for whom “Vice, accidents, and terrible ends are his speciality.” Even the most absurd disaster “would not surprise” him, and “The only way you could really astonish him would be by living a blameless life without adventure.” He expects the worst so completely that only an uneventful life would surprise him.

A.why_wrong: The text describes what Gustus expects of others’ lives, not adventures of his own or stories he tells about them.

B.why_wrong: Gustus expects disaster, but the text never says he is afraid of it or avoids risks himself.

C.why_wrong: A blameless, uneventful life would “astonish” Gustus because he does not expect one, not because he admires it.

sources.what: Stella Benson, This Is the End (1917), paragraph on Cousin Gustus, copied exactly from Project Gutenberg eBook 11324

items.notes: Literary prose, character portrait; key names the trait and its comic consequence. Distractors: invented behavior, expectation misread as fear, astonishment misread as admiration.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg 11324: exact.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Rose Macaulay’s 1912 novel The Lee Shore. Peter Margerison, a newcomer at an English boarding school, intensely admires Urquhart, an older student and a celebrated member of the school’s football team. A fifteen cap is a cap awarded to members of that team, and lines are a punishment requiring a student to copy out writing.

Did Urquhart know that he, Margerison, was in fact Margerison? Peter never expected it.

But a few days after that, Urquhart looked round and said, “I say, you—Margerison. Just cut down to the field and bring my cap.”

Peter cut along quick, and found the velvet tasselled thing and brought it and hung it up with the care due to a thing so precious as a fifteen cap. The school bell had clanged while he was down on the field, and he was late and had lines. That didn’t matter. The thing that had emerged was, Urquhart knew he was Margerison.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Peter resents being sent on an errand that makes him late for class and earns him a punishment.
Peter is so delighted that Urquhart knows who he is that being punished for lateness hardly matters to him.
Peter hopes that running errands for Urquhart will eventually earn him a place on the football team.
Peter worries that Urquhart will be angry with him if the precious cap is damaged on the way back.
items.explanation: Peter “never expected” Urquhart to know who he was, so when Urquhart calls him “Margerison,” Peter is thrilled. He is “late and had lines,” but “That didn’t matter,” because “Urquhart knew he was Margerison.” His delight at being recognized outweighs the punishment.

A.why_wrong: The text says the lateness and lines “didn’t matter” to Peter, so he does not resent the errand.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Peter hopes to join the team; what matters to him is that Urquhart knows his name.

D.why_wrong: Peter handles the cap with care because it is “so precious,” but the text never says he fears Urquhart’s anger.

sources.what: Rose Macaulay, The Lee Shore (1912), chapter 1; text from Project Gutenberg eBook 16612

items.notes: Literary prose. Adapted: opening 'Then there was another aspect: did' recast as 'Did'; two sentences of the first paragraph and the cap's location dropped; '--' set as a closed em dash. Glosses for fifteen cap and lines added to the context line.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg 16612: opening recast, 'He showed no sign...' sentence, 'Peter came into the lavatories and found Urquhart there, and' and the cap's location cut (the writer's note omits the lavatories cut); wording otherwise exact.

items.passage: To learn why mosquitoes seem to prefer some people, Maria Elena De Obaldia, Leslie Vosshall, and colleagues had volunteers wear nylon sleeves on their forearms for six hours, then let Aedes aegypti mosquitoes choose between pairs of sleeves. Because only the sleeves were offered, cues such as body heat and exhaled carbon dioxide played no part. Some volunteers’ sleeves drew far more mosquitoes than others did, and the rankings stayed stable when the volunteers were retested over several years. The most attractive volunteers’ skin also gave off much higher levels of compounds called carboxylic acids.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most likely be concluded about why some people attract more mosquitoes than others?
options: It likely depends on how much body heat and carbon dioxide a person gives off.
It likely shifts from month to month as people change their diets and habits.
It likely reflects a lasting difference in the odor of people’s skin.
It likely results from mosquitoes learning to prefer people they have bitten before.
items.explanation: Only the worn sleeves were offered, so “body heat and exhaled carbon dioxide played no part”: skin odor alone produced the differences. Because “the rankings stayed stable when the volunteers were retested over several years,” the difference in odor is a lasting one rather than a passing condition.

A.why_wrong: The text says body heat and carbon dioxide “played no part” in the sleeve tests, yet the differences still appeared.

B.why_wrong: The rankings “stayed stable” over several years, so the attraction did not shift from month to month.

D.why_wrong: The mosquitoes chose between worn sleeves; the text never mentions earlier bites or mosquitoes learning preferences.

sources.what: De Obaldia et al. 2022, Cell: skin odor collected on nylon sleeves worn on forearms for 6 hours; two-choice assays with Aedes aegypti; temperature and CO2 held constant; differences in attraction stable over several years; highly attractive people produce more skin carboxylic acids

items.notes: Natural science (entomology). P1: odor alone drove the differences; P2: rankings stable over years; conclusion: a lasting skin-odor difference. All options hedged with 'likely'.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the Cell abstract (PMC10069481): differences stable over several years; attractive people produce more carboxylic acids.

items.passage: Kim Man-deok was an eighteenth-century merchant on Jeju, an island off the southern coast of Korea. By trading commodities such as seaweed, pearls, and grain, she accumulated enough wealth to become one of the richest people in the kingdom. In the 1790s, repeated crop failures and violent storms caused a devastating famine on Jeju, and several vessels transporting rice from the mainland were wrecked. Kim then spent most of her fortune purchasing rice and distributing it to the island’s starving inhabitants, preserving thousands of lives.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Kim do when famine struck Jeju?
options: She spent most of her wealth on rice for the island’s hungry people.
She sailed to the mainland to ask the government for help.
She sold rice to the people of Jeju at a lower price than usual.
She paid for new vessels to replace the ones that had been wrecked.
items.explanation: The text says that Kim “spent most of her fortune purchasing rice and distributing it to the island’s starving inhabitants.” Choice A restates this.

B.why_wrong: The text never says Kim traveled to the mainland or asked the government for help.

C.why_wrong: Kim distributed the rice to the starving inhabitants; the text does not say she sold it.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions wrecked vessels, but not that Kim replaced them.

sources.what: Kim Man-deok (Gim Man-deok): Jeju merchant who traded local goods and grain and became one of the richest people in Joseon; famine from 1792 with crop failures, storms, and wrecked relief boats; used most of her fortune to buy and distribute rice, saving many lives

items.notes: History. Easy explicit detail; key paraphrases one sentence.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia (Gim Man-deok): famine from 1792, relief boats wrecked, she used most of her fortune to buy and distribute rice.

items.passage: Composer William Grant Still grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas, where his stepfather took him to performances and purchased recordings of classical music for him. He subsequently studied at Oberlin Conservatory and composed nearly two hundred works. In 1931 the Rochester Philharmonic performed his Symphony No. 1, “Afro-American,” the first time a major orchestra had played a complete score by an African American composer. In 1936 Still conducted the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Hollywood Bowl, becoming the first African American to lead a major American orchestra.
items.stem: According to the text, what was significant about Still’s 1936 performance at the Hollywood Bowl?
options: It was the first time his Symphony No. 1 was performed.
It was the very first concert that his stepfather had ever taken him to see.
It led him to begin his studies at Oberlin Conservatory.
It made him the first African American to lead a major American orchestra.
items.explanation: The text says that in 1936 Still conducted the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Hollywood Bowl, “becoming the first African American to lead a major American orchestra.”

A.why_wrong: Symphony No. 1 was performed in 1931 by the Rochester Philharmonic, five years earlier.

B.why_wrong: His stepfather took him to performances when he was growing up in Little Rock, not to the 1936 concert.

C.why_wrong: Still studied at Oberlin before his symphony was performed in 1931, so the 1936 concert could not have led him there.

sources.what: William Grant Still: stepfather took him to operettas and bought classical recordings; studied at Oberlin; nearly 200 works; Afro-American Symphony performed 1931 by the Rochester Philharmonic, the first complete score by an African American played by a major orchestra; conducted the Los Angeles Philharmonic at the Hollywood Bowl in 1936

items.notes: Arts (music). Easy explicit detail. Not the abolitionist William Still of an official Transitions item.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia: 1936 Hollywood Bowl, first African American to conduct a major American symphony orchestra (lead). Distinct from the abolitionist William Still of the official Transitions item.

items.passage: During the Antarctic winter, emperor penguins endure frigid temperatures by huddling together, sometimes so tightly that individual birds cannot move independently. Yet each penguin requires time in the sheltered interior of the group, not merely on its exposed perimeter. To understand how the birds accomplish this, researcher Daniel Zitterbart and his team studied huddles at a penguin colony. They discovered that every 30 to 60 seconds, all the penguins take small steps simultaneously, and these steps travel through the huddle like a wave. Gradually, the tiny movements reorganize the entire group.
items.stem: According to the text, how do the penguins in a tightly packed huddle manage to move?
options: The penguins on the outer edge push their way into the interior one at a time.
All the penguins take small steps at the same time, creating a wave.
The huddle breaks apart every minute so that the penguins can trade places.
The largest penguins make room by stepping out of the huddle.
items.explanation: Zitterbart’s team discovered that “every 30 to 60 seconds, all the penguins take small steps simultaneously, and these steps travel through the huddle like a wave.” Choice B restates this.

A.why_wrong: The text describes all the penguins moving together, not those on the perimeter pushing inward one by one.

C.why_wrong: The steps happen every 30 to 60 seconds, but the huddle stays together; it does not break apart.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions penguin size or birds leaving the huddle.

sources.what: Zitterbart et al. 2011, PLoS ONE: emperor penguins huddle so tightly that individual movements become impossible; each needs time inside the huddle; every 30-60 seconds all penguins make small steps that travel as a wave through the huddle; small moves lead to large-scale reorganization

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Easy explicit detail; key paraphrases one sentence.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the PLoS ONE abstract (PMC3106014).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Juhani Aho’s 1883 short story “When Father Brought Home the Lamp” (translated by R. Nisbet Bain). A Finnish farmer proposes purchasing an oil lamp to replace the resinous pine splinters, called pare wood, that his household burns for illumination.

“And you’ll lose nothing by the lamp, either! Pare wood costs money too, and you can’t find it everywhere on our land now as you used to.”

Mother knew well enough that pare wood is not so quickly used up as all that, as nothing had been said about it up to now, and that it was only an excuse to go away and buy this lamp. But she wisely held her tongue so as not to vex father, for then the lamp and all would have been unbought and unseen.
items.stem: According to the text, why does Mother keep quiet about Father’s reason for buying the lamp?
options: She agrees that pare wood has become hard to find on their land.
She worries that an oil lamp might set the house on fire.
She does not want to annoy Father and lose the chance to have a lamp.
She plans to buy a lamp for the family herself on her next trip to town.
items.explanation: Mother knows Father’s reason is “only an excuse,” but she “held her tongue so as not to vex father, for then the lamp and all would have been unbought and unseen.” She keeps quiet so that she does not upset him and lose the lamp.

A.why_wrong: Mother knows that pare wood “is not so quickly used up as all that,” so she does not agree with Father’s reason.

B.why_wrong: The excerpt never mentions any fear of fire.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say Mother plans to buy a lamp herself; it is Father who wants to go and buy it.

sources.what: Juhani Aho, 'When Father Brought Home the Lamp' (from Squire Hellman, translated by R. Nisbet Bain), in Stories by Foreign Authors: Scandinavian, Project Gutenberg eBook 5336
Siihen aikaan kun isä lampun osti, 1883

items.notes: Literary prose, easy explicit detail (why does X). Adapted: Father's speech cut after 'as you used to.' Context line explains pare wood (the source footnote calls it a resinous pine chip used instead of torch or candle).

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg 5336 (story title and Bain translation as in the source): exact, Father's speech cut after 'as you used to.'

items.passage: Many adults address infants in parentese, a slow, high-pitched style of speech with exaggerated intonation. Naja Ferjan Ramírez, Patricia Kuhl, and colleagues investigated whether coaching parents to converse with their infants more frequently, and in parentese, would influence the infants’ language development. One group of families received coaching when the infants were 6 and 10 months old, while another group received none. The coached parents used more parentese at home, and their infants babbled more. By 14 months, those infants were also producing more words than infants in the other group.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that babies pay more attention to parentese than to ordinary adult speech.
Researchers think that parents should stop using parentese once their babies start to speak.
An experiment showed that most parents already use parentese without being taught to.
An experiment showed that coaching parents in how to talk to babies may help the babies learn to talk.
items.explanation: Infants whose parents were coached “babbled more” and by 14 months “were also producing more words than infants in the other group.” Choice D states this main finding.

A.why_wrong: The study measured infants’ babbling and words, not whether they paid more attention to parentese.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when parents should stop using parentese.

C.why_wrong: The coached parents used more parentese than before, and the text never says most parents already use it without coaching.

sources.what: Ferjan Ramirez, Lytle, Fish and Kuhl 2019, Developmental Science: randomized trial; coaching at 6 and 10 months on child-directed speech, back-and-forth turns and parentese; coached parents used more parentese; intervention infants babbled more and produced more words at 14 months than controls

items.notes: Social science (child language). Study report with the finding in the last two sentences; key abstracts it with a hedge.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the Developmental Science abstract (PubMed 30318708; 2019 issue, online 2018). claims.txt line said 2020: CORRECTION line appended.

items.passage: For thousands of years, people have extracted salt from deep inside the mountains near Hallstatt, Austria. The salt has preserved many materials the miners left behind, including their excrement. Frank Maixner and his team analyzed these remains to determine what the miners consumed. Most samples revealed a diet dominated by grains and beans. However, one sample from the Iron Age contained abundant DNA from two fungi used to make blue cheese and beer. It provides the first DNA evidence that people in Iron Age Europe consumed blue cheese and beer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Remains preserved in a salt mine offer the first DNA evidence that Iron Age Europeans ate blue cheese and drank beer.
Salt miners near Hallstatt ate mostly cheese and beer because grains were difficult to grow high in the mountains.
Researchers have found that salt taken from the Hallstatt mines was once used in making both cheese and beer.
Researchers learned that miners at Hallstatt were the first people in the world to make blue cheese.
items.explanation: Maixner’s team analyzed remains preserved by the salt and found that one Iron Age sample contained DNA “from two fungi used to make blue cheese and beer,” which provides “the first DNA evidence that people in Iron Age Europe consumed blue cheese and beer.” Choice A states this finding.

B.why_wrong: The text says most samples revealed “a diet dominated by grains and beans,” not mostly cheese and beer.

C.why_wrong: The salt preserved the miners’ remains; the text never says it was used to make cheese or beer.

D.why_wrong: The finding is the first DNA evidence for Iron Age Europe, not proof that these miners were the first anywhere to make blue cheese.

sources.what: Maixner et al. 2021, Current Biology: paleofeces preserved in Hallstatt salt mines from the Bronze Age to the 18th century; diet of cereals (bran, glumes) and broad beans; one Iron Age sample rich in Penicillium roqueforti and Saccharomyces cerevisiae DNA, the first molecular evidence for blue cheese and beer consumption in Iron Age Europe

items.notes: Archaeology. Easy study report; main idea in the last two sentences. Passage keeps the finding to one sample, as the source does.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed in the Current Biology abstract (PMC8660109).

items.passage: Nigerian artist and architect Demas Nwoko studied fine arts in Zaria and theatrical design in Paris, and throughout his career he has combined contemporary techniques with African traditions. When he needed a residence and studio in Ibadan in the 1960s but lacked funds, he constructed them himself from bricks of clay and laterite, a reddish soil, obtained from the site. His first major building, a chapel for a Dominican mission in Ibadan, was designed to remain cool inside despite the city’s intense sunlight. In 2023 he received a lifetime achievement award at the Venice Architecture Biennale.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Nwoko is best known for the theatrical designs he created while he was studying in Paris.
Nwoko built his own home because no architect in Ibadan was willing to work for him.
Nwoko designs buildings that suit their surroundings, using local materials and planning for local conditions.
Nwoko has designed more chapels in Nigeria than any other architect of his time.
items.explanation: Nwoko built his home and studio from “clay and laterite, a reddish soil, obtained from the site,” and designed his chapel “to remain cool inside despite the city’s intense sunlight.” Both examples show that he designs buildings suited to their surroundings.

A.why_wrong: Nwoko studied theatrical design in Paris, but the text never says he is best known for designs from that time.

B.why_wrong: The text says he built his home himself because he “lacked funds,” not because no architect would work for him.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions only one chapel and makes no comparison with other architects.

sources.what: Demas Nwoko: studied fine arts at Zaria and stage design in Paris; combines modern techniques with African tradition; built his Ibadan house and studio from clay and laterite found on site when short of money; first major building for the Dominican mission in Ibadan, designed for interior coolness against Ibadan's sun; 2023 Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, Venice Architecture Biennale

items.notes: Arts (architecture). Profile: training and approach, two examples, recognition. Key generalizes the examples.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed on Wikipedia: clay and laterite from the site when short of money; Dominican chapel designed for Ibadan's sun; 2023 Golden Lion.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Elizabeth Stuart Phelps’s 1869 short story “No News.” Harrie and Dr. Sharpe, a physician, are newlyweds living in a seaside community.

Dr. Sharpe used to drive home by the beach, on a fair night, always, that he might see [Harrie in her boat at sunset]. Then Harrie would row swiftly in, and spring into the low, broad buggy beside him, and they rode home together in the fragrant dusk. Sometimes she used to chatter on these twilight drives; but more often she crept up to him and shut her eyes, and was as still as a sleepy bird. It was so pleasant to do nothing but be happy!
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Harrie is tired from rowing and wishes her husband had come to meet her sooner.
Harrie feels peaceful and content when she rides home with her husband in the evening.
Harrie talks the whole way home because she wants to tell her husband about her day.
Dr. Sharpe drives home along the beach because it is the fastest route back to their house.
items.explanation: On the drives home, Harrie usually “crept up to him and shut her eyes, and was as still as a sleepy bird,” and the text adds, “It was so pleasant to do nothing but be happy!” She feels calm and content riding home with her husband.

A.why_wrong: Harrie “would row swiftly in” to meet him; nothing suggests she is tired or impatient with her husband.

C.why_wrong: She only “Sometimes” chattered; “more often” she was quiet and still.

D.why_wrong: The text says he took the beach road “that he might see” Harrie in her boat, not because it was faster.

sources.what: Elizabeth Stuart Phelps, 'No News', in Men, Women, and Ghosts (Fields, Osgood, 1869), Project Gutenberg eBook 10744

items.notes: Literary prose, easy. Adapted: 'it' (the sight of Harrie in her boat at sunset, from the previous paragraph) replaced with a bracketed phrase.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg 10744: exact apart from the bracketed replacement of 'it'.
